given: First token probabilities: sun 0.55, rain 0.45. Given sun: end 0.4, more 0.6. Given rain: end 0.9, more 0.1.
These are complete toy branches; end paths stop, more paths do not.
topic_evidence.mechanism: Conditional probabilities describe what follows a particular prefix. Multiplying along a path gives its joint probability. The four branch products sum to 1, but the two end paths sum to 0.625 because more branches have not ended. Greedy decoding selects sun then more; it does not guarantee the most likely complete sequence.
topic_evidence.independent_question: First tokens go=0.4, wait=0.35, ask=0.25. End probabilities given them are 0.5,0.8,1 respectively; each branch has a complementary more token. Compute all three end-path probabilities and their sum. Which first token is greedy, which end path is largest, and does either verify a real status?
topic_evidence.independent_answer: Teacher explanation: End-path probabilities 0.2,0.28,0.25; sum 0.73. Greedy first token is go, but wait,end is the largest of the specified end paths. Neither establishes a real status without appropriate evidence.

given: At T=1, A=0.8 and B=0.2. For positive T use p^(1/T), then normalise.

given: Schema: exactly title text, pages integer, source_id text. Approved record R: River Notes, 64 pages.

topic_evidence.mechanism: Returning passes a value back to the caller. Local names belong to a function call; storing the returned value creates a separate caller binding.
topic_evidence.independent_question: Trace both calls and the final expression. If return total is removed from the function, does this final print complete? Would a separate print(total) outside the function have access to its local variable?
topic_evidence.independent_answer: With the return: first=6, second=10, sum16, so output is6 10 16. Removing the return makes both calls return None; evaluating first+second raises TypeError before print runs, so no line is printed. In this shown program total is local, so an outside print(total) raises NameError. Each call has its own local computation.
